Printing for DMAR Result Tables

Source: R/dmar_tbl.R
dmar_tbl.Rd

Most DMAR estimation and testing functions return a tidy data.frame with a term column and one or more numeric columns. Because a single numeric column often holds quantities on very different scales (for example, whole-number degrees of freedom alongside an F statistic, an effect size, and a small p-value), the base print.data.frame method formats the whole column with one common format and is easily pushed into scientific notation with many trailing digits. The dmar_tbl class supplies print and format methods that format each value on its own terms: whole numbers (such as degrees of freedom and sample sizes) print without a decimal part, other values print to a fixed number of decimal places, and no value is shown in scientific notation.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'dmar_tbl'
format(
  x,
  digits = getOption("dmar.digits", 3L),
  digits_p = 4L,
  digits_fixed = 3L,
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'dmar_tbl'
print(
  x,
  digits = getOption("dmar.digits", 3L),
  digits_p = 4L,
  digits_fixed = 3L,
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'dmar_tbl'
rbind(..., deparse.level = 1)

Arguments

x

A dmar_tbl object (a data.frame returned by a DMAR function).

digits

Number of decimal places for values that are not whole numbers, and for measured values that are (see Details): a single whole number of 0 or more. Defaults to getOption("dmar.digits", 3L). A class whose display lays out cells of its own, or writes numbers in the lines beneath the table, uses the same digits there.

digits_p

Number of decimal places for p-values. Defaults to 4. A p-value below 10^(-digits_p) prints as “< 0.0001” (with the threshold tracking digits_p).

digits_fixed

Number of decimal places for fixed_terms rows (information criteria such as AIC and BIC, and log-likelihoods). Defaults to 3.

...

For print(), additional arguments passed to print.data.frame. For rbind(), the tables to stack, and any of the named arguments of rbind.data.frame (make.row.names, stringsAsFactors, factor.exclude).

deparse.level

For rbind(): passed to rbind.data.frame, which does not use it for data frames. It keeps its base R spelling because rbind() supplies it by that name.

Value

print.dmar_tbl returns x invisibly. format.dmar_tbl returns a data.frame whose numeric columns have been formatted to character for display. rbind() of DMAR tables returns a dmar_tbl when every table stacked has the same classes and attributes, and an ordinary data.frame otherwise (see the section on stacking).

Details

The stored numeric values are never rounded; only their display changes, so downstream arithmetic on the returned object (confidence interval widths, further calculations) uses full precision.

The same formatting applies to every dmar_tbl, whether the table is long (a term column beside a single value or estimate column) or wide (a leading label column such as term, effect, or sample_type beside several typed numeric columns). Each numeric column is formatted on its own terms, so the shape of the table does not matter.

Display precision is a number of decimal places, three by default, set by the digits argument or, globally, by options(dmar.digits = ). (The option is dot-named because that is the R convention for package options, for example dplyr.width and knitr.table.format; it is not a function or argument name and so is outside the package's snake_case rule.) A value that is not a whole number prints to that many decimal places with its trailing zeros, so every such value in a column shows the same number of decimal places: 13.018 prints as 13.018, 0.56 as 0.560, 233.4107 as 233.411, and 1.5 as 1.500. A value too small for those decimals prints as 0.000 rather than in scientific notation (0.000123 and 3.35e-52 both print as 0.000), and a value that rounds to zero prints as 0.000 whatever its sign, never as -0.000.

A whole number prints without a decimal part, as a count (degrees of freedom, a sample size, a number of replications) does. A measured quantity can land on a whole number as well, at the bound of its range or where it is fixed, and it then prints to the decimal places of the values of its kind beside it. The display recognizes a measured value in four ways.

  • A bound and the estimate it belongs to. A row or column named ci_lower or ci_upper, or with a name ending in _lower or _upper, is a bound: a confidence limit (tau2_ci_lower, rmsea_ci_upper, cles_ci_lower, smd_ci_lower), and in the same way an equivalence bound (smd_lower, contrast_upper) or a one-sided test statistic (t_upper). The estimate an interval belongs to is the row or column its limits are named for (tau2, rmsea), the row of a long table that its ci_lower and ci_upper rows belong to (the estimate results_sentence reports), the column tidy takes as the estimate of a wide table with limit columns, and a row whose own limits sit beside it in limit columns (the ci_lower and ci_upper of a coefficient table). So a lower limit of exactly 0 reads 0.000 beside an upper limit of 0.083, and a loading fixed at 1 reads 1.000 beside its interval.

  • A measured kind, wherever it appears. A fit index (CFI, TLI, RMSEA, SRMR, and the others, with their differences between models); a power; a proportion, probability, or fraction (the pct_ rows of a sensitivity analysis, a coverage, an assurance, a fraction of missing information); a mean, median, standard deviation, variance, or higher moment (the mean_, median_, and sd_ rows of a sensitivity analysis); a test statistic, a standard error, or a noncentrality parameter; the delta and the weights of a model comparison; and the heterogeneity indices of a meta-analysis. So a CFI of 1 reads 1.000 beside a TLI of 1.012, a power of 1 reads 1.000 beside a power of 0.840, and a standard deviation of the interval widths of 0 reads 0.000 beside their mean of 1.176. A name that also names a count, such as delta_df or median_N, is a count.

  • A column of measured values. A column that holds values that are not whole is measured throughout, so an F of 4 reads 4.000 beside 4.270 and a standard error of 0 reads 0.000 beside 0.050. The exception is a column named for a count, with n, N, df, or B as its name or as a part of its name (df_2, N_effective), which counts its whole values even when others are not whole (degrees of freedom adjusted for sphericity read 2 beside 1.830), and a row that records the table's sum-of-squares type. The value or estimate column beside a term column is not read this way, since it can hold a different quantity on each row.

  • A row or column the producing function names. A function names the rows or columns that hold measured values of its own kind through a measured_terms attribute (the congruence coefficients of factor_congruence, the loadings and intercepts of dmacs).

Elsewhere a whole number prints without a decimal part. That covers the counts, the codes and indicators (the sum-of-squares type, whether an equivalence test concluded equivalence), and a value the call was given as a whole number, since nothing in a table says which of its other whole numbers are counts: in a long table the value column holds a sample size of 301 on one row and, on another, a planning value given as 15, which prints as 15.

p-values are shown to a number of decimal places of their own (four by default, set by digits_p), which is the conventional way to report them. A p-value smaller than the smallest magnitude those decimals can represent prints as “< 0.0001” instead of rounding to 0.0000. A column is treated as holding p-values when it is named p_value, p.value, p_adjusted (the multiplicity-adjusted case, as in ci_dunnett), or p_chi_square (the exact-fit test of a fitted model, as in measurement_invariance); in a long-format table whose quantities share a single value column, the rows to format this way are named by the producing function through a p_terms attribute. The limits of an interval for a p-value, rows named for it with _ci_lower and _ci_upper (the Monte Carlo interval of the bootstrap p-value of sem_exact_fit_bootstrap), print to the same decimal places, without the floor, since a limit of 0 is a limit and not a p-value below the smallest that can be shown.

Information criteria such as AIC and BIC, and log-likelihoods, keep a number of decimal places of their own, digits_fixed (three by default), which digits does not change, so a model comparison difference of a few points is not rounded away when the rest of a table is shown to fewer decimals; such a value prints its decimals even when it is a whole number. The producing function names these rows through a fixed_terms attribute.

A table that carries a bootstrap attribute (the reliability family's bootstrap intervals; see reliability_alpha) prints one more line stating how many replications were attempted, how many returned a value, and why the rest were set aside, so the replications the interval conditions on are always on the page.

A table that carries a denominator attribute (the omega coefficients of reliability_omega, reliability_omega_categorical, and bifactor_indices) prints a line naming how the total variance in the denominator was estimated, and a table that carries a residual_cor attribute prints the largest residual correlation of the single-factor fit with the item pair it belongs to (or, for a three-item fit, says that the saturated model leaves no residual correlation to read), so the coefficient on the page is identified without reference to a default and the local dependence beside it is in view. The knitr methods (knit_print.dmar_tbl and as_kable) write the same lines with a knitted table, as they do the lines a result adds of its own (for example which version of a fit measure sem_fit_measures reported and why), so a report shows what the console shows.

A sample size plan made for incomplete data (ss_aipe_reliability with fmi above 0) prints a line naming the fraction of missing information it assumed and the sample size complete data would need, and a sensitivity analysis that planned for or simulated missing data (ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity with fmi or missing_prop above 0) prints a line naming both, so the assumptions behind the number stay beside it. In the same way, an assurance plan of ss_aipe_c made with a nonzero true_kurtosis prints a line naming the excess kurtosis of the errors its assurance allows for.

To see more precision than the display shows, raise digits (print(x, digits = 8) shows eight decimal places) or read the columns directly, since the stored values are never rounded: x$value or x[["p_value"]] returns the numbers at full precision.

Using the result in your own code

You do not need to know anything about S3 classes to use a dmar_tbl. It is an ordinary data.frame with a print method, so everything you already do with a data frame works: x$value pulls the numeric column, x[x$term == "smd", ] selects a row, and the full-precision numbers are right there for any further calculation. Three common needs:

  • Read one number. Index it like any data frame, for example x$value[x$term == "ci_upper"]. The display rounds; the stored value does not, so this returns the number at full precision.

  • See more (or fewer) decimal places. Use print(x, digits = 6) for a single table, or options(dmar.digits = 6) for the rest of the session.

  • Hand the result to other tools. tidy(x) returns a one-row-per-term table in DMAR's own column vocabulary (term, estimate, se, statistic, p_value, ci_lower, ci_upper, and so on), which is the convenient “wide” view for plotting or joining; glance(x) returns a one-row model-level summary. Both come from the generics package and need no extra setup. For a single-estimand result such as ci_smd the table is already one row, so glance() coincides with tidy() (there are no extra model-level statistics to report); for a multi-row result such as mlmr they differ.

Stacking tables with rbind()

A dmar_tbl carries facts about its numbers as attributes: the confidence level, which rows are p-values, and whatever else its function recorded (dmar_metadata lists them). The lines printed beneath a table are written from those attributes, so a stacked table can keep them only when they are true of every row. rbind() of DMAR tables therefore returns

  • a dmar_tbl of the same class and with the same attributes, when every table stacked is a dmar_tbl and all of them have identical classes and attributes (two calls of one function at one confidence level, for example);

  • an ordinary data.frame with the same rows and columns and none of the DMAR attributes, in every other case: tables at different confidence levels, tables from different functions, or a DMAR table stacked with a plain data frame. No warning is given. The numbers are all there; what is dropped is the class and the attributes, so that no printed line states a confidence level (or anything else) that does not hold for every row.

To compare results across confidence levels, stack the tidy() rows instead, which carry the level in a conf_level column: rbind(tidy(x_90), tidy(x_95)). NULL arguments are ignored, as rbind() ignores them. dplyr::bind_rows() does not call this method, so what is said here does not apply to it; use rbind(), or stack tidy() rows.

See also

tidy and glance for the wide one-row-per-term and the one-row summary views. For a gentle, non-technical tour of how to read and use DMAR result tables, see the “Reading DMAR result tables” vignette: vignette("dmar_output", package = "DMAR").

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# Every DMAR estimation function returns a table that prints this way.
x <- ci_smd(smd = 0.5, n_1 = 50, n_2 = 50)
x                       # rounded for reading, to three decimal places
#>  term     value
#>  ci_lower 0.101
#>  smd      0.500
#>  ci_upper 0.897
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# The stored numbers keep full precision; only the display rounds.
x$value[x$term == "smd"]
#> [1] 0.5
print(x, digits = 8)    # ask the display for more decimal places
#>  term     value     
#>  ci_lower 0.10058571
#>  smd      0.50000000
#>  ci_upper 0.89694143
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# Pull a single number out, exactly as you would from a data frame.
x$value[x$term == "ci_upper"]
#> [1] 0.8969414

# The broom verbs give the programmer-friendly wide and summary views.
generics::tidy(x)
#>   term estimate  ci_lower  ci_upper conf_level
#> 1  smd      0.5 0.1005857 0.8969414       0.95
generics::glance(x)
#>   term estimate  ci_lower  ci_upper conf_level
#> 1  smd      0.5 0.1005857 0.8969414       0.95

# The same display rules apply to a wide table, one with several typed
# columns, for example an effect size with its confidence interval per
# effect.
ci_eta_squared(aov(iq_8 ~ treatment, data = pygmalion))
#>  effect    eta_squared_total eta_squared_total_ci_lower
#>  treatment 0.020             0.001                     
#>  eta_squared_total_ci_upper eta_squared_partial eta_squared_partial_ci_lower
#>  0.061                      0.020               0.001                       
#>  eta_squared_partial_ci_upper F_value df_effect df_error N  
#>  0.061                        6.335   1         308      310
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# Stacking two tables computed at different confidence levels gives an
# ordinary data frame, because no one confidence level describes every
# row. The tidy() rows keep each level in a column.
x_90 <- ci_smd(smd = 0.5, n_1 = 50, n_2 = 50, conf_level = 0.90)
class(rbind(x, x_90))
#> [1] "data.frame"
rbind(generics::tidy(x), generics::tidy(x_90))
#>   term estimate  ci_lower  ci_upper conf_level
#> 1  smd      0.5 0.1005857 0.8969414       0.95
#> 2  smd      0.5 0.1645872 0.8329100       0.90
